title: Query Caching
description: Apply result-set caching, materialized views, and cache invalidation strategies

data.text: Query caching avoids repeated computation by storing result sets or precomputed aggregates. Choosing the right cache layer and invalidation strategy is essential for data freshness.

data.title: Options
items: Database buffer cache: automatic page cache
Query result cache: application or ORM level

data.title: Materialized view for reports
data.code:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_sales AS
SELECT
  DATE(created_at) AS sale_date,
  SUM(total) AS daily_total,
  COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATE(created_at);

-- Refresh on schedule or trigger
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_sales;

data.title: Tip
data.text: Prefer time-based invalidation for slowly changing dimensions. For frequently updated data, use event-driven invalidation or short TTLs.

items.question: Is query caching always good?
items.answer: No. Caching adds complexity and risk of stale data. Cache only proven expensive queries.

items.question: When should I use materialized views?
items.answer: For expensive aggregations over large tables where near-real-time freshness is acceptable.

items.question: How do I invalidate caches safely?
items.answer: Use write-through or cache-aside patterns. Invalidate on data changes, not on a timer.

data.title: Summary
points: Prefer external caches for shared data
data.takeaway: Query caching trades freshness for speed. Match the cache strategy to the data volatility and query cost.
